request: Is a QALY a QALY, whoever gets it? Part 2: The old and the disabled

sources.title: QALYfying the value of life
sources.finding: QALYs discriminate against the old and the disabled

commands.speak: Now that we have seen the case for weighting every QALY equally, look at who ends up with fewer QALYs to gain.
Say a cure saves a life, and afterwards the person lives to 80 at a quality of 0.8 — illustrative numbers.
Saved at 30, that is fifty years at 0.8: forty QALYs.
Saved at 70, the same cure buys ten years: eight QALYs.
Same treatment, same cost, but the older patient's rescue counts for a fifth as much.
Now a young patient with a lasting disability, living at 0.4 after the cure.
The same fifty years give only twenty QALYs: half the priority, because of the disability.
In 1987 the philosopher John Harris attacked exactly this, in a paper called 'QALYfying the value of life'.
His point: each person who wants to go on living has the same claim to it, however many QALYs their life holds.
Critics call the disability case double jeopardy: the first misfortune lowers your quality of life, and then it lowers your priority.
Defenders reply that the QALY counts health gained, not the worth of a person, and that ignoring it means buying less health overall.
So QALYs do not rank people, but wherever there is less health to gain, the old and the disabled come second.
